one_liner: Seven teaching kernels written with libstdc++ std::experimental::simd, timed against de-vectorized scalar loops on x86-64, AArch64 and RVV.
what_it_does: A study repository, not a library: each of seven exercises (add and memory-bound FMA, sum and dot product, upper-bound clamp, count above threshold, stable softmax, 3-tap horizontal blur, 1D valid convolution) has a scalar version in src/scalar and a std::experimental::simd version in src/simd with identical free-function signatures over raw float pointers. Drivers in drivers/ generate seeded inputs, check results against a reference copy, and write CSV timings; per-exercise docs explain the masks, loads, tails and reductions used.
how_it_is_fast: Plain explicit vectorization with native_simd<float> (16 lanes under AVX-512, 4 on M1 NEON, fixed 4 or 8 on the RISC-V toolchain): copy_from/copy_to unaligned loads and stores, one lane-wise accumulator plus stdx::reduce or stdx::hmax for reductions, stdx::fma for dot product, where() masks for clamp and popcount(mask) for counting, three shifted loads for the blur and broadcast weights for the convolution, with scalar tails. There are no multi-accumulator tricks, prefetching, non-temporal stores or vector exp; most of the clamp and count gains come from replacing branchy scalar decisions with masks.
when_to_use: Learning or teaching std::experimental::simd idioms (where, popcount on masks, reduce, hmax, shifted loads) from short, documented examples.
Copying a small reduction kernel (float sum or dot product) where you cannot use -ffast-math; these are the rows GCC would not auto-vectorize at -O3 anyway (5.37x sum on the Xeon with GCC).
Checking how one std::experimental::simd source behaves across AVX-512, NEON and RVV toolchains, including the README's notes on what each compiler actually emitted.
Starting point for a portable stencil or FIR kernel when you are already on GCC/libstdc++ and want to avoid intrinsics.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that std::simd beats normally optimized code: every scalar row is built with -fno-tree-vectorize (GCC) or -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize (icpx), and no plain -O3 scalar row exists, so add, FMA, clamp, blur and convolution gains are likely much smaller against an ordinary build.
When you need a maintained library: 0 stars, history from 2026-09-03, no releases, no packaging, no API stability; for production use EVE, Vector Class Library or ISPC.
Toolchains without libstdc++ <experimental/simd> (Apple Clang/libc++, MSVC) or code meant for C++26 <simd>, which the repo does not use.
Transcendental-heavy work: softmax's exp loop stays scalar std::exp, so softmax gains are only 1.2x to 2.35x.
Memory-bound streaming (add, FMA): gains are 1.01x to 2.60x because the kernels are traffic-limited.

integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (-std=c++2b) with libstdc++ <experimental/simd>; tested with GCC 14.1, Homebrew GCC 15.2.0, conda-forge GCC 16.2 (RISC-V cross) and icpx 2025.2
integration.platforms: x86-64 (Makefile defaults assume AVX-512 on MareNostrum 5), AArch64 (Apple M1 with Homebrew GCC), RISC-V RVV 1.0 (cross-compiled; native_simd<float> reports one lane, so fixed widths 4 and 8 were used in separate, unpublished builds)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the kernels are stateless free functions over caller-owned buffers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — each SIMD kernel keeps the same signature as its scalar twin and can be copied, but there is no library target, header-only package or versioned API

gotchas: Harness asymmetry beyond the documented de-vectorized baseline: the SIMD binaries are compiled with auto-vectorization on, so the SIMD column also includes whatever the compiler vectorizes in the source's plain loops (the README notes icpx turns softmax's scalar exp loop into SVML calls, which only the SIMD build can do).

Clamp's scalar side is a branchy conditional store on uniform [-1, 1] data with bound 0.5 (about 25% taken, random), and count tests > 0 on the same distribution (about 50%); the 6.81x/10.29x x86 and 20.00x/24.51x M1 clamp/count rows largely measure removed branch mispredictions against a baseline the compiler was told not to vectorize.

Weak softmax validation: the driver accepts a max absolute difference of 1e-2 while each output for 4,194,304 standard-normal logits is at most about 3e-5 (my estimate), so only the sum-to-one checksum (within 1e-3) guards correctness; the kernel itself looks correct on reading.

Kernels do not check preconditions: convolve_1d computes input_size - kernel_size + 1 in size_t and blur_horizontal assumes width >= 2; only the drivers validate. Clamp and softmax drivers keep 10 full copies of the input (640 MiB for clamp at the default 16,777,216 floats); no result CSVs are committed (results/ is gitignored), and x86 rows for exercises 1-5 predate the per-sample warm-up change.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over EVE or the Vector Class Library only when you want short worked examples of the standard std::experimental::simd API rather than a supported SIMD library; like UltraSIMD and libalgebra, its speedups are measured against deliberately non-vectorized scalar code, so do not use its ratios to choose between libraries.
verified_claims_summary: On one pinned core of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ with GCC 14.1, std::experimental::simd versions ran faster than scalar builds compiled with -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns by 5.37x (sum), 5.89x (1D convolution), 6.81x (clamp), 4.85x (count), 1.78x (dot product) and 1.04x (memory-bound FMA), median of 9 samples of 10 calls; icpx 2025.2, an unpinned Apple M1 Pro with GCC 15.2.0 (up to 24.51x on count) and a Banana Pi F3 (RVV, VL=8, 4.51x sum) were also measured. Only the sum and dot-product rows plausibly survive against a plain -O3 build, since GCC does not reassociate float reductions without -ffast-math.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-10-06, 89 commits, all since 2026-09-03), MIT-licensed teaching code with 0 stars, no issues and no releases; small enough to copy single kernels, but treat it as documentation of std::experimental::simd rather than a dependency.
